# ===========================================================================
# The store
# ===========================================================================
# The invariants that make it correct:
#
#   1. Write-ahead: a record is in the log, and synced, before the memtable
#      changes and before put or delete returns. So every acknowledged
#      write survives a crash, and a crash loses at most the one write that
#      was in flight.
#   2. The log is a clean prefix: recovery replays records while they are
#      whole, checksummed and numbered seq, seq + 1, ... and cuts the log
#      at the first one that is not, so new records never follow garbage.
#   3. Snapshot plus log: the snapshot holds every record up to its seq,
#      and the log holds the records after it (perhaps some before it too,
#      which recovery skips). The snapshot only ever appears whole,
#      because it is synced under a temporary name and then renamed.


class StoreError(Exception):
    """A request the store cannot carry out."""


class CorruptFile(StoreError):
    """A file that was written whole fails its checks: damage, not a crash."""


class RecoveryReport(NamedTuple):
    replayed: int            # PUT and DELETE records applied from the log
    dropped: int             # bytes cut from the end of the log
    problem: str | None      # why replay stopped early, or None

    def __str__(self):
        text = f"replayed {self.replayed} records"
        if self.problem:
            text += f"; dropped {self.dropped} bytes ({self.problem} tail)"
        return text


def check_key(key):
    if not isinstance(key, str):
        raise TypeError("a key must be a string")
    if not key:
        raise ValueError("a key must not be empty")


def check_value(value):
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        raise TypeError("a value must be a string")


class KVStore:
    """A durable map from non-empty string keys to string values."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        fs,
        name="db",
        wal_limit=None,
        seed=0,
    ):
        self.fs = fs
        self.name = name
        self.wal = name + ".wal"
        self.snap = name + ".snap"
        self.wal_limit = wal_limit       # checkpoint when the log grows past this
        self.seed = seed
        self.mem = SkipList(seed)        # the live keys, sorted
        self.seq = 0                     # sequence number of the last record
        self.checkpoints = 0             # checkpoints taken since opening
        self.closed = False
        self.recovery = self._recover()

    # -- recovery -------------------------------------------------------------

    def _recover(self):
        """Rebuild the in-memory state from the files, and tidy them."""
        if self.fs.exists(self.snap + ".tmp"):
            self.fs.delete(self.snap + ".tmp")   # a checkpoint that crashed
        if self.fs.exists(self.snap):
            self.seq, table = decode_snapshot(self.fs.read(self.snap))
            for key, value in sorted(table.items()):
                self.mem.put(key, value)
        return self._replay_wal()

    def _replay_wal(self):
        """Apply the log to the memtable, stopping at the first bad record,
        and cut the log back to the end of the last good one."""
        if not self.fs.exists(self.wal):
            return RecoveryReport(0, 0, None)
        data = self.fs.read(self.wal)
        offset = 0              # end of the last good record
        replayed = 0
        problem = None
        while offset < len(data):
            try:
                record, end = decode_record(data, offset)
            except TornRecord:
                problem = "torn"
                break
            except CorruptRecord:
                problem = "corrupt"
                break
            if record.seq <= self.seq and replayed == 0:
                offset = end    # already in the snapshot
                continue
            if record.seq != self.seq + 1:
                problem = "gap"         # a record is missing: nothing after it can be trusted
                break
            self._apply(record)
            self.seq = record.seq
            replayed += 1
            offset = end
        dropped = len(data) - offset
        if dropped:
            self.fs.truncate(self.wal, offset)   # so new records follow good ones
        return RecoveryReport(replayed, dropped, problem)

    def _apply(self, record):
        """Make one PUT or DELETE record true in the memtable."""
        if record.kind == PUT:
            self.mem.put(record.key, record.value)
        else:
            self.mem.delete(record.key)

    # -- the log ----------------------------------------------------------------

    def _log(self, kind, key="", value=""):
        """Append the next record to the log. Not yet durable: sync after."""
        record = Record(self.seq + 1, kind, key, value)
        self.fs.append(self.wal, encode_record(record))
        self.seq = record.seq
        return record

    def _write(self, kind, key, value=""):
        """Log one record, make it durable, and only then apply it."""
        record = self._log(kind, key, value)
        self.fs.sync(self.wal)
        self._apply(record)
        self._maybe_checkpoint()

    def wal_size(self):
        """How many bytes the log holds."""
        return self.fs.size(self.wal) if self.fs.exists(self.wal) else 0

    def _check_open(self):
        if self.closed:
            raise StoreError("the store is closed")

    # -- reading ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        """The value stored under key, or default."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        return self.mem.get(key, default)

    def __contains__(self, key):
        return self.get(key) is not None

    def scan(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """The (key, value) pairs with lo <= key < hi, in key order."""
        self._check_open()
        return list(self.mem.items(lo, hi))

    def count(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """How many keys k have lo <= k < hi."""
        self._check_open()
        return sum(1 for _ in self.mem.items(lo, hi))

    def items(self):
        return self.scan()

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.mem)

    # -- writing ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def put(self, key, value):
        """Store value under key. Durable when put returns."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        check_value(value)
        self._write(PUT, key, value)

    def delete(self, key):
        """Remove key. Returns True if it was there. Durable when it returns."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        if key not in self.mem:
            return False
        self._write(DELETE, key)
        return True

    # -- checkpoints ----------------------------------------------------------------

    def _maybe_checkpoint(self):
        if self.wal_limit is not None and self.wal_size() > self.wal_limit:
            self.checkpoint()

    def checkpoint(self):
        """Save the whole table as a snapshot, then empty the log.

        Crash-safe at every step: before the rename the old snapshot and the
        full log are there; after it, the new snapshot holds every record
        still in the log, and recovery skips them by sequence number.
        """
        self._check_open()
        self.checkpoints += 1
        write_atomically(self.fs, self.snap, encode_snapshot(self.mem.items(), self.seq))
        if self.wal_size():
            self.fs.truncate(self.wal, 0)

    def close(self):
        self.closed = True
--- solution
"""A key-value store with a write-ahead log, crash recovery and a query language.

The layers, from the bottom up:

  records      the binary record: length, CRC32 checksum, sequence number
  MemFS        a simulated file system that can crash after any byte
  KVStore      an in-memory table, made durable by a write-ahead log
  SSTable      a sorted, immutable file with an index
  SkipList     the sorted in-memory table, for range scans
  LSM tree     the memtable flushes to SSTables listed in a manifest
"""
from bisect import bisect_right
import heapq
import random
import struct
import zlib
from typing import NamedTuple


# ===========================================================================
# Records
# ===========================================================================
# Every file this store writes is made of records. On disk, one record is:
#
#     length   u32   how many bytes the body has
#     crc      u32   zlib.crc32 of the body
#     body:
#       seq    u64   sequence number: 1, 2, 3, ... in the order written
#       kind   u8    what the record does: PUT, DELETE, ...
#       klen   u32   length of the key in bytes (UTF-8)
#       vlen   u32   length of the value in bytes (UTF-8)
#       key    klen bytes
#       value  vlen bytes
#
# All integers are little-endian ("<" in struct).

HEADER = struct.Struct("<II")    # length, crc
BODY = struct.Struct("<QBII")    # seq, kind, klen, vlen
MAX_BODY = 1 << 24               # 16 MiB: a longer body is damage, not data

PUT = 1
DELETE = 2
KINDS = {PUT, DELETE}


class Record(NamedTuple):
    seq: int
    kind: int
    key: str
    value: str = ""


class RecordError(Exception):
    """The bytes at an offset are not one whole, valid record."""


class TornRecord(RecordError):
    """The data ends before the record does: the last write was cut short."""


class CorruptRecord(RecordError):
    """All of the record's bytes are there, but they are damaged."""


def encode_record(record):
    """The bytes of one record: the header, then the body."""
    key = record.key.encode("utf-8")
    value = record.value.encode("utf-8")
    body = BODY.pack(record.seq, record.kind, len(key), len(value)) + key + value
    if len(body) > MAX_BODY:
        # Never write what decode_record would reject: it would be lost.
        raise ValueError(f"record of {len(body)} bytes is larger than {MAX_BODY}")
    return HEADER.pack(len(body), zlib.crc32(body)) + body


def decode_record(data, offset=0):
    """Decode the record that starts at data[offset].

    Returns (record, end), where end is the offset just past the record.
    Raises TornRecord if the data stops before the record ends, and
    CorruptRecord if the record is complete but fails a check.
    """
    left = len(data) - offset
    if left < HEADER.size:
        raise TornRecord(f"offset {offset}: {left} of {HEADER.size} header bytes")
    length, crc = HEADER.unpack_from(data, offset)
    if length < BODY.size or length > MAX_BODY:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: impossible body length {length}")
    start = offset + HEADER.size
    end = start + length
    if end > len(data):
        raise TornRecord(f"offset {offset}: body of {length} bytes, {len(data) - start} there")
    body = bytes(data[start:end])
    if zlib.crc32(body) != crc:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: checksum mismatch")
    seq, kind, klen, vlen = BODY.unpack_from(body)
    if kind not in KINDS:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: unknown kind {kind}")
    if BODY.size + klen + vlen != length:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: key and value lengths do not add up")
    try:
        key = body[BODY.size:BODY.size + klen].decode("utf-8")
        value = body[BODY.size + klen:].decode("utf-8")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: text is not valid UTF-8") from None
    return Record(seq, kind, key, value), end


def read_records(data):
    """Decode records from the start of data, stopping at the first bad one.

    Returns (records, good_end, problem). good_end is the offset just past
    the last good record. problem is None when all of data was good, "torn"
    when it ends in a cut-off record, and "corrupt" when a record is damaged.
    """
    records = []
    offset = 0
    while offset < len(data):
        try:
            record, end = decode_record(data, offset)
        except TornRecord:
            return records, offset, "torn"
        except CorruptRecord:
            return records, offset, "corrupt"
        records.append(record)
        offset = end
    return records, offset, None


# ===========================================================================
# A file system that can crash
# ===========================================================================
class SimulatedCrash(Exception):
    """The simulated machine died in the middle of an operation.

    Store code must never catch this: a real crash cannot be caught either.
    """


class MemFS:
    """An in-memory file system that can crash after any byte.

    Every byte written is one step, and so is each sync, rename, truncate
    and delete. With budget=k exactly k steps happen: the machine crashes
    when step k + 1 is tried, part-way through a write if need be.
    budget=None never crashes. `steps` counts the steps taken, so one run
    with no budget measures a workload.

    The program sees every byte it has written. crash() gives the files a
    restarted machine finds: every written byte after a process crash, only
    the synced bytes after a power loss.
    """

    def __init__(self, budget=None):
        self.files = {}      # name -> bytearray: what the program sees
        self.synced = {}     # name -> how many leading bytes are durable
        self.budget = budget
        self.steps = 0
        self.crashed = False

    # -- the crash machinery ------------------------------------------------

    def _allow(self, n):
        """Take up to n steps; return how many the budget allows."""
        if self.crashed:
            raise SimulatedCrash("the machine has already crashed")
        if self.budget is None:
            allowed = n
        else:
            allowed = max(0, min(n, self.budget - self.steps))
        self.steps += allowed
        return allowed

    def _die(self):
        self.crashed = True
        raise SimulatedCrash(f"crashed after {self.steps} steps")

    def _step(self):
        if self._allow(1) < 1:
            self._die()

    def _need(self, name):
        if name not in self.files:
            raise FileNotFoundError(name)

    # -- reading costs no steps --------------------------------------------

    def exists(self, name):
        return name in self.files

    def names(self):
        return sorted(self.files)

    def size(self, name):
        self._need(name)
        return len(self.files[name])

    def read(self, name):
        self._need(name)
        return bytes(self.files[name])

    def read_at(self, name, offset, size):
        """Up to size bytes from offset on (fewer at the end of the file)."""
        self._need(name)
        return bytes(self.files[name][offset:offset + size])

    # -- writing: every byte and every operation is a step -----------------

    def append(self, name, data):
        """Add bytes to the end of a file, creating it if needed."""
        allowed = self._allow(len(data))
        if name not in self.files:
            self.files[name] = bytearray()
            self.synced[name] = 0
        self.files[name] += data[:allowed]
        if allowed < len(data):
            self._die()

    def sync(self, name):
        """Make every byte written to the file so far durable (fsync)."""
        self._need(name)
        self._step()
        self.synced[name] = len(self.files[name])

    def rename(self, old, new):
        """Give a file a new name in one atomic step, replacing any file there."""
        self._need(old)
        self._step()
        self.files[new] = self.files.pop(old)
        self.synced[new] = self.synced.pop(old)

    def truncate(self, name, size):
        """Cut a file down to its first size bytes."""
        self._need(name)
        if not 0 <= size <= len(self.files[name]):
            raise ValueError(f"cannot truncate {name} to {size} bytes")
        self._step()
        del self.files[name][size:]
        self.synced[name] = min(self.synced[name], size)

    def delete(self, name):
        self._need(name)
        self._step()
        del self.files[name]
        del self.synced[name]

    # -- crashing -------------------------------------------------------------

    def crash(self, power_loss=False):
        """The files a restarted machine finds, as a new MemFS with no budget."""
        after = MemFS()
        for name, data in self.files.items():
            keep = self.synced[name] if power_loss else len(data)
            after.files[name] = bytearray(data[:keep])
            after.synced[name] = keep
        return after

    def listing(self):
        """One line per file: name, size, and how much of it is synced."""
        return "\n".join(f"{name}  {len(self.files[name])} bytes, {self.synced[name]} synced"
                         for name in self.names())

    def __repr__(self):
        state = "crashed" if self.crashed else f"{self.steps} steps"
        return f"<MemFS {len(self.files)} files, {state}>"

    def attempt(self, fn):
        """Run fn(). True if it finished, False if this file system crashed."""
        try:
            fn()
        except SimulatedCrash:
            if not self.crashed:
                raise
        return not self.crashed


def append_record(fs, name, record):
    """Append one record to a log file and make it durable."""
    fs.append(name, encode_record(record))
    fs.sync(name)


def load_records(fs, name):
    """The good records at the start of a log file ([] if there is no file)."""
    if not fs.exists(name):
        return []
    return read_records(fs.read(name))[0]


KIND_NAMES = {PUT: "PUT", DELETE: "DELETE"}


def describe_log(data):
    """A listing of log bytes for people debugging: one line per record with
    its offset, sequence number, kind, key and value, then what (if
    anything) is wrong with the tail."""
    lines = []
    offset = 0
    while offset < len(data):
        try:
            record, end = decode_record(data, offset)
        except TornRecord:
            lines.append(f"{offset:>6}  torn: {len(data) - offset} bytes not used")
            break
        except CorruptRecord:
            lines.append(f"{offset:>6}  corrupt: {len(data) - offset} bytes not used")
            break
        text = f"{offset:>6}  #{record.seq} {KIND_NAMES[record.kind]}"
        if record.key:
            text += f" {record.key!r}"
        if record.kind == PUT:
            text += f" = {record.value!r}"
        lines.append(text)
        offset = end
    return "\n".join(lines)


def write_atomically(fs, name, data):
    """Write a whole file so that `name` is either untouched or complete.

    The bytes go to a temporary file, which is synced, then renamed over
    `name`. A crash at any step leaves the old file (or none) in place.
    """
    tmp = name + ".tmp"
    if fs.exists(tmp):
        fs.delete(tmp)      # left over from a write that crashed
    fs.append(tmp, data)
    fs.sync(tmp)            # durable before it gets the real name
    fs.rename(tmp, name)


# ===========================================================================
# SSTables: sorted, immutable files with an index
# ===========================================================================
# Costs, for n entries and an index of every B-th key: opening a table
# reads the footer and n/B index keys; get does a binary search of the
# index, O(log(n/B)) comparisons, then decodes at most B entries; a scan
# of m entries decodes about m + B. The file never changes after it is
# written, so it needs no locking and can be copied or cached freely.
#
# An SSTable holds entries in key order, each one a record (PUT, or DELETE
# for a tombstone), then a sparse index, then a fixed-size footer:
#
#     data     entry 0, entry 1, ..., entry n-1
#     index    for every index_every-th entry: u32 key length, key, u64 offset
#     footer   magic b"KVSST001", u64 index offset, u64 index entries,
#              u64 entry count, u64 seq, u32 crc32 of the index,
#              u32 crc32 of the footer bytes before this field

SST_MAGIC = b"KVSST001"
SST_FOOTER = struct.Struct("<8sQQQQII")
U32 = struct.Struct("<I")
U64 = struct.Struct("<Q")


def write_sstable(fs, name, entries, seq, index_every=16):
    """Write (key, value) entries, in strictly increasing key order, as an
    SSTable. A value of None is a tombstone. The file appears atomically."""
    if index_every < 1:
        raise ValueError("index_every must be at least 1")
    data = bytearray()
    index = bytearray()
    index_count = 0
    count = 0
    previous = None
    for key, value in entries:
        if previous is not None and key <= previous:
            raise ValueError(f"keys must be strictly increasing: {previous!r} then {key!r}")
        previous = key
        if count % index_every == 0:
            raw = key.encode("utf-8")
            index += U32.pack(len(raw)) + raw + U64.pack(len(data))
            index_count += 1
        if value is None:
            data += encode_record(Record(seq, DELETE, key))
        else:
            data += encode_record(Record(seq, PUT, key, value))
        count += 1
    head = SST_FOOTER.pack(SST_MAGIC, len(data), index_count, count, seq, zlib.crc32(index), 0)[:-4]
    footer = head + U32.pack(zlib.crc32(head))
    write_atomically(fs, name, bytes(data + index + footer))


class SSTable:
    """Reads one SSTable file. Only the footer and the index live in memory;
    entries are read from the file when needed."""

    def __init__(self, fs, name):
        self.fs = fs
        self.name = name
        size = fs.size(name)
        if size < SST_FOOTER.size:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{name}: too short to be an SSTable")
        footer = fs.read_at(name, size - SST_FOOTER.size, SST_FOOTER.size)
        magic, index_at, index_count, count, seq, index_crc, footer_crc = SST_FOOTER.unpack(footer)
        if magic != SST_MAGIC or zlib.crc32(footer[:-4]) != footer_crc:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{name}: bad footer")
        index_end = size - SST_FOOTER.size
        if index_at > index_end:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{name}: index offset past the end")
        raw = fs.read_at(name, index_at, index_end - index_at)
        if zlib.crc32(raw) != index_crc:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{name}: index checksum mismatch")
        self.keys = []       # every index_every-th key, in order
        self.offsets = []    # where each of those entries starts
        pos = 0
        for _ in range(index_count):
            (klen,) = U32.unpack_from(raw, pos)
            self.keys.append(raw[pos + 4:pos + 4 + klen].decode("utf-8"))
            (offset,) = U64.unpack_from(raw, pos + 4 + klen)
            self.offsets.append(offset)
            pos += 4 + klen + 8
        self.data_end = index_at
        self.count = count
        self.seq = seq
        self.reads = 0       # entries decoded so far, for tests of the cost

    def __len__(self):
        return self.count

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"<SSTable {self.name!r}: {self.count} entries, seq {self.seq}>"

    def _entry(self, offset):
        """The entry at offset, and the offset of the next one."""
        head = self.fs.read_at(self.name, offset, HEADER.size)
        if len(head) < HEADER.size or offset + HEADER.size > self.data_end:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{self.name}: entry at {offset} runs past the data")
        (length, _) = HEADER.unpack(head)
        raw = head + self.fs.read_at(self.name, offset + HEADER.size, length)
        try:
            record, size = decode_record(raw)
        except RecordError as error:
            raise CorruptFile(f"{self.name}: {error}") from None
        self.reads += 1
        return record, offset + size

    def _block(self, key):
        """The index slot of the last indexed key <= key (-1 if key is before them all)."""
        return bisect_right(self.keys, key) - 1

    def get(self, key):
        """The entry for key (a PUT or DELETE record), or None if there is none.
        Binary search on the index, then at most one block of entries."""
        slot = self._block(key)
        if slot < 0:
            return None
        offset = self.offsets[slot]
        end = self.offsets[slot + 1] if slot + 1 < len(self.offsets) else self.data_end
        while offset < end:
            record, offset = self._entry(offset)
            if record.key == key:
                return record
            if record.key > key:
                return None
        return None

    def items(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """(key, value) for every entry with lo <= key < hi, in key order.
        value is None for a tombstone. None for lo or hi means no bound."""
        offset = 0
        if lo is not None and self._block(lo) >= 0:
            offset = self.offsets[self._block(lo)]
        while offset < self.data_end:
            record, offset = self._entry(offset)
            if lo is not None and record.key < lo:
                continue
            if hi is not None and record.key >= hi:
                return
            yield record.key, (record.value if record.kind == PUT else None)


# ===========================================================================
# The skip list: a sorted map in memory
# ===========================================================================
# Costs, for n keys: get, put and delete take O(log n) expected time, since
# each level holds about half the nodes of the one below, so a search makes
# about two moves per level on about log2(n) levels. The random heights
# come from a seeded generator, so a run can be repeated exactly. A scan of
# m keys costs O(log n + m): one search, then a walk along level 0.
class _Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "value", "next")

    def __init__(self, key, value, height):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.next = [None] * height    # next[i]: the following node on level i


class SkipList:
    """A sorted map with expected O(log n) get, put and delete.

    Level 0 links every node in key order. Each node also joins level 1
    with probability 1/2, level 2 with probability 1/4, and so on, so a
    search runs along the high levels first and skips most nodes.
    `visits` counts the nodes searches step onto, for tests of the cost.
    """

    MAX_LEVEL = 24

    def __init__(self, seed=0):
        self.head = _Node(None, None, self.MAX_LEVEL)
        self.level = 1       # levels in use
        self.size = 0
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
        self.visits = 0

    def __len__(self):
        return self.size

    def __iter__(self):
        return (key for key, _ in self.items())

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"<SkipList {self.size} keys, {self.level} levels>"

    def _random_height(self):
        height = 1
        while height < self.MAX_LEVEL and self.rng.random() < 0.5:
            height += 1
        return height

    def _before(self, key):
        """For every level, the last node whose key is less than key."""
        before = [self.head] * self.MAX_LEVEL
        node = self.head
        for level in range(self.level - 1, -1, -1):
            while node.next[level] is not None and node.next[level].key < key:
                node = node.next[level]
                self.visits += 1
            before[level] = node
        return before

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        node = self._before(key)[0].next[0]
        if node is not None and node.key == key:
            return node.value
        return default

    def __contains__(self, key):
        node = self._before(key)[0].next[0]
        return node is not None and node.key == key

    def put(self, key, value):
        """Insert key, or replace its value if it is already there."""
        before = self._before(key)
        node = before[0].next[0]
        if node is not None and node.key == key:
            node.value = value
            return
        height = self._random_height()
        self.level = max(self.level, height)
        node = _Node(key, value, height)
        for level in range(height):
            node.next[level] = before[level].next[level]
            before[level].next[level] = node
        self.size += 1

    def delete(self, key):
        """Remove key. Returns True if it was there."""
        before = self._before(key)
        node = before[0].next[0]
        if node is None or node.key != key:
            return False
        for level in range(len(node.next)):
            before[level].next[level] = node.next[level]
        while self.level > 1 and self.head.next[self.level - 1] is None:
            self.level -= 1
        self.size -= 1
        return True

    def check(self):
        """The broken invariants, as a list of text (empty when all is well):
        each level is sorted, each level's nodes are also on the level below,
        and level 0 holds size nodes."""
        problems = []
        below = None
        for level in range(self.level):
            keys = []
            node = self.head.next[level]
            while node is not None:
                keys.append(node.key)
                node = node.next[level]
            if any(a >= b for a, b in zip(keys, keys[1:])):
                problems.append(f"level {level} is not strictly sorted")
            if below is not None and not set(keys) <= below:
                problems.append(f"level {level} has keys missing from level {level - 1}")
            if level == 0 and len(keys) != self.size:
                problems.append(f"level 0 has {len(keys)} nodes, size says {self.size}")
            below = set(keys)
        return problems

    def items(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """(key, value) pairs with lo <= key < hi, in key order."""
        node = self.head.next[0] if lo is None else self._before(lo)[0].next[0]
        while node is not None and (hi is None or node.key < hi):
            yield node.key, node.value
            node = node.next[0]

    def clear(self):
        """Remove every key. The nodes are taken apart one at a time: in the
        browser, freeing a chain of thousands of nodes in one go overflows
        the stack."""
        node = self.head.next[0]
        self.head = _Node(None, None, self.MAX_LEVEL)
        self.level = 1
        self.size = 0
        while node is not None:
            after = node.next[0]
            node.next = None             # cut this node loose
            node = after


def prefix_end(prefix):
    """The smallest string greater than every string that starts with prefix,
    or None when there is none (the empty prefix, or only U+10FFFF).
    Keys starting with prefix are exactly those with prefix <= key < end."""
    chars = list(prefix)
    while chars:
        last = ord(chars.pop())
        if last < 0x10FFFF:
            chars.append(chr(last + 1))
            return "".join(chars)
    return None


# ===========================================================================
# Merging sorted runs, and the manifest
# ===========================================================================
# The manifest names the SSTables that make up the store, newest first:
#
#     magic   8 bytes  b"KVMAN001"
#     seq     u64      every log record up to seq is in the tables
#     next    u64      the number for the next table file
#     count   u32      how many table names follow
#     names   count times: u32 length, name (UTF-8)
#     crc     u32      zlib.crc32 of every byte before it

MANIFEST_MAGIC = b"KVMAN001"
MANIFEST_HEAD = struct.Struct("<8sQQI")


def encode_manifest(seq, next_table, names):
    out = bytearray(MANIFEST_HEAD.pack(MANIFEST_MAGIC, seq, next_table, len(names)))
    for name in names:
        raw = name.encode("utf-8")
        out += U32.pack(len(raw)) + raw
    out += U32.pack(zlib.crc32(out))
    return bytes(out)


def decode_manifest(data):
    """(seq, next_table, table names) from manifest bytes; CorruptFile if bad."""
    if len(data) < MANIFEST_HEAD.size + 4 or zlib.crc32(data[:-4]) != U32.unpack_from(data, len(data) - 4)[0]:
        raise CorruptFile("manifest checksum mismatch")
    magic, seq, next_table, count = MANIFEST_HEAD.unpack_from(data)
    if magic != MANIFEST_MAGIC:
        raise CorruptFile("not a manifest")
    names = []
    pos = MANIFEST_HEAD.size
    for _ in range(count):
        (length,) = U32.unpack_from(data, pos)
        names.append(data[pos + 4:pos + 4 + length].decode("utf-8"))
        pos += 4 + length
    if pos != len(data) - 4:
        raise CorruptFile("manifest has bytes after its names")
    return seq, next_table, names


def merge_runs(runs):
    """Merge sorted runs of (key, value) pairs, given newest first.

    Yields every key once, in key order, with the value from the newest run
    that has it (None for a tombstone). A heap holds the front pair of each
    run, so k runs with n pairs in all cost O(n log k).
    """
    iterators = [iter(run) for run in runs]
    heap = []

    def push(i):
        pair = next(iterators[i], None)
        if pair is not None:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (pair[0], i, pair[1]))

    for i in range(len(iterators)):
        push(i)
    while heap:
        key, i, value = heapq.heappop(heap)
        push(i)
        while heap and heap[0][0] == key:       # older versions of the same key
            _, j, _ = heapq.heappop(heap)
            push(j)
        yield key, value


# ===========================================================================
# The store
# ===========================================================================
# The invariants that make it correct:
#
#   1. Write-ahead: a record is in the log, and synced, before the memtable
#      changes and before put or delete returns. So every acknowledged
#      write survives a crash, and a crash loses at most the one write that
#      was in flight.
#   2. The log is a clean prefix: recovery replays records while they are
#      whole, checksummed and numbered seq, seq + 1, ... and cuts the log
#      at the first one that is not, so new records never follow garbage.
#   3. Tables plus log: the manifest names the SSTables and the seq they
#      cover; the log holds the records after it (perhaps some before it
#      too, which recovery skips). Files appear whole, because each one is
#      synced under a temporary name and then renamed, and the manifest
#      rename is the single moment a flush or a compaction takes effect.
#   4. Newest wins: the memtable is newer than every table, and tables are
#      kept newest first, so the first layer that has a key decides it. A
#      tombstone (None) in a newer layer hides the key in older ones.


class StoreError(Exception):
    """A request the store cannot carry out."""


class CorruptFile(StoreError):
    """A file that was written whole fails its checks: damage, not a crash."""


class RecoveryReport(NamedTuple):
    replayed: int            # PUT and DELETE records applied from the log
    dropped: int             # bytes cut from the end of the log
    problem: str | None      # why replay stopped early, or None

    def __str__(self):
        text = f"replayed {self.replayed} records"
        if self.problem:
            text += f"; dropped {self.dropped} bytes ({self.problem} tail)"
        return text


def check_key(key):
    if not isinstance(key, str):
        raise TypeError("a key must be a string")
    if not key:
        raise ValueError("a key must not be empty")


def check_value(value):
    if not isinstance(value, str):
        raise TypeError("a value must be a string")


_MISSING = object()          # "not in this layer", as opposed to a tombstone


class KVStore:
    """A durable map from non-empty string keys to string values."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        fs,
        name="db",
        wal_limit=None,
        index_every=16,
        seed=0,
    ):
        self.fs = fs
        self.name = name
        self.wal = name + ".wal"
        self.manifest = name + ".manifest"
        self.wal_limit = wal_limit       # checkpoint when the log grows past this
        self.index_every = index_every
        self.seed = seed
        self.mem = SkipList(seed)        # key -> value, or None for a tombstone
        self.tables = []                 # open SSTables, newest first
        self.next_table = 1              # number for the next table file
        self.seq = 0                     # sequence number of the last record
        self.checkpoints = 0             # checkpoints taken since opening
        self.closed = False
        self.recovery = self._recover()

    # -- recovery -------------------------------------------------------------

    def _recover(self):
        """Rebuild the in-memory state from the files, and tidy them."""
        self._load_manifest()
        self._remove_orphans()
        return self._replay_wal()

    def _replay_wal(self):
        """Apply the log to the memtable, stopping at the first bad record,
        and cut the log back to the end of the last good one."""
        if not self.fs.exists(self.wal):
            return RecoveryReport(0, 0, None)
        data = self.fs.read(self.wal)
        offset = 0              # end of the last good record
        replayed = 0
        problem = None
        while offset < len(data):
            try:
                record, end = decode_record(data, offset)
            except TornRecord:
                problem = "torn"
                break
            except CorruptRecord:
                problem = "corrupt"
                break
            if record.seq <= self.seq and replayed == 0:
                offset = end    # already in the snapshot
                continue
            if record.seq != self.seq + 1:
                problem = "gap"         # a record is missing: nothing after it can be trusted
                break
            self._apply(record)
            self.seq = record.seq
            replayed += 1
            offset = end
        dropped = len(data) - offset
        if dropped:
            self.fs.truncate(self.wal, offset)   # so new records follow good ones
        return RecoveryReport(replayed, dropped, problem)

    def _apply(self, record):
        """Make one PUT or DELETE record true in the memtable."""
        if record.kind == PUT:
            self.mem.put(record.key, record.value)
        else:
            self.mem.put(record.key, None)       # a tombstone hides older tables

    # -- the log ----------------------------------------------------------------

    def _log(self, kind, key="", value=""):
        """Append the next record to the log. Not yet durable: sync after."""
        record = Record(self.seq + 1, kind, key, value)
        self.fs.append(self.wal, encode_record(record))
        self.seq = record.seq
        return record

    def _write(self, kind, key, value=""):
        """Log one record, make it durable, and only then apply it."""
        record = self._log(kind, key, value)
        self.fs.sync(self.wal)
        self._apply(record)
        self._maybe_checkpoint()

    def wal_size(self):
        """How many bytes the log holds."""
        return self.fs.size(self.wal) if self.fs.exists(self.wal) else 0

    def _check_open(self):
        if self.closed:
            raise StoreError("the store is closed")

    # -- reading ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _lookup(self, key):
        """The newest value of key in any layer: None if absent or deleted."""
        value = self.mem.get(key, _MISSING)
        if value is not _MISSING:
            return value
        for table in self.tables:            # newest first: the first hit wins
            record = table.get(key)
            if record is not None:
                return record.value if record.kind == PUT else None
        return None

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        """The value stored under key, or default."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        value = self._lookup(key)
        return default if value is None else value

    def __contains__(self, key):
        return self.get(key) is not None

    def _merged(self, lo, hi):
        """Every layer merged: (key, value or None) in key order."""
        runs = [self.mem.items(lo, hi)] + [table.items(lo, hi) for table in self.tables]
        return merge_runs(runs)

    def scan(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """The live (key, value) pairs with lo <= key < hi, in key order."""
        self._check_open()
        return [(k, v) for k, v in self._merged(lo, hi) if v is not None]

    def count(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """How many live keys k have lo <= k < hi."""
        self._check_open()
        return sum(1 for _, v in self._merged(lo, hi) if v is not None)

    def items(self):
        return self.scan()

    def keys(self, lo=None, hi=None):
        """The live keys with lo <= key < hi, in key order, one at a time."""
        self._check_open()
        return (k for k, v in self._merged(lo, hi) if v is not None)

    def __iter__(self):
        return self.keys()

    def __len__(self):
        return self.count()

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"<KVStore {self.name!r}: seq {self.seq}, {len(self.tables)} tables>"

    # -- writing ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def put(self, key, value):
        """Store value under key. Durable when put returns."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        check_value(value)
        self._write(PUT, key, value)

    def delete(self, key):
        """Remove key. Returns True if it was there. Durable when it returns."""
        self._check_open()
        check_key(key)
        if self._lookup(key) is None:
            return False
        self._write(DELETE, key)
        return True

    # -- checkpoints ----------------------------------------------------------------

    def _maybe_checkpoint(self):
        if self.wal_limit is not None and self.wal_size() > self.wal_limit:
            self.checkpoint()

    def _table_name(self, number):
        return f"{self.name}-{number:06d}.sst"

    def checkpoint(self):
        """Flush the memtable to a new SSTable, record it in the manifest, and
        empty the log. Each step is safe to crash in: a table the manifest
        does not name is deleted by recovery, and log records up to the
        manifest's seq are skipped."""
        self._check_open()
        self.checkpoints += 1
        if len(self.mem):
            entries = list(self.mem.items())
            if not self.tables:
                # Nothing older to hide, so tombstones can go.
                entries = [(k, v) for k, v in entries if v is not None]
            name = self._table_name(self.next_table)
            self.next_table += 1
            write_sstable(self.fs, name, entries, self.seq, self.index_every)
            self.tables.insert(0, SSTable(self.fs, name))
        self._save_manifest()
        if self.wal_size():
            self.fs.truncate(self.wal, 0)
        self.mem = SkipList(self.seed)

    def table_names(self):
        """The SSTable files, newest first."""
        return [table.name for table in self.tables]

    def _save_manifest(self):
        data = encode_manifest(self.seq, self.next_table, self.table_names())
        write_atomically(self.fs, self.manifest, data)

    def _load_manifest(self):
        """Open the tables the manifest names; seq becomes its checkpoint seq."""
        if not self.fs.exists(self.manifest):
            return
        self.seq, self.next_table, names = decode_manifest(self.fs.read(self.manifest))
        self.tables = [SSTable(self.fs, name) for name in names]

    def _remove_orphans(self):
        """Delete files a crash left behind: temporary files, and tables the
        manifest does not name."""
        live = set(self.table_names())
        for name in self.fs.names():
            ours = name.startswith(self.name + "-") and (name.endswith(".sst") or name.endswith(".sst.tmp"))
            if (ours and name not in live) or name == self.manifest + ".tmp":
                self.fs.delete(name)

    def close(self):
        self.closed = True
--- hint
`merge_runs`: make a list of iterators with `iter(run)`, and a small inner function `push(i)` that takes the next pair of run `i` (with `next(it, None)`) and pushes `(key, i, value)`. Push once per run. Then loop: pop, push the same run again, pop and discard (pushing their runs) while the heap's smallest key equals this key, then yield.
--- hint
Give the store a private `_lookup(key)` that returns the newest value in any layer, or `None` for absent or deleted. The memtable needs a sentinel to tell "not in this layer" (keep looking) from a tombstone (stop): `value = self.mem.get(key, _MISSING)` with `_MISSING = object()`. `get` and `delete` both use `_lookup`; `scan` merges `[self.mem.items(lo, hi)] + [t.items(lo, hi) for t in self.tables]`.
--- hint
Recovery order: load the manifest (tables, `seq`, `next_table`), then remove orphans by comparing `fs.names()` with the set of table names, then the old log replay, which already skips records up to `seq`.

+++ practice | Merging sorted lists with a heap
--- task
Write `merge_sorted(lists)` that merges any number of lists, each already sorted from smallest to largest, into one sorted list, using `heapq`. Keep duplicates. When equal values come from different lists, the value from the list that comes first in `lists` comes out first. It must cost O(n log k) for n values in k lists: do not concatenate and sort.

For example, `merge_sorted([[1, 4, 9], [2, 3], [], [4]])` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 9]`.
--- starter
import heapq


def merge_sorted(lists):
    out = []
    for values in lists:
        out += values
    return out
--- solution
import heapq


def merge_sorted(lists):
    heap = [(values[0], i, 0) for i, values in enumerate(lists) if values]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        value, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(value)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out
--- hint
Keep one entry per list on the heap: `(value, list number, position in that list)`. The list number breaks ties, so the earlier list's value pops first.
--- hint
Pop the smallest entry, append its value, and push the next value of the same list, if it has one.
--- check case | The example from the task
merge_sorted([[1, 4, 9], [2, 3], [], [4]])
=> [1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 9]
--- check case | No lists, and only empty lists
(merge_sorted([]), merge_sorted([[], []]))
=> ([], [])
--- check test | Ties come out in the order of the lists
(lambda T: [t.tag for t in merge_sorted([[T(1, "a1"), T(2, "a2")], [T(1, "b1"), T(2, "b2")]])] == ["a1", "b1", "a2", "b2"])(type("T", (), {"__init__": lambda s, v, tag: (setattr(s, "v", v), setattr(s, "tag", tag))[0], "__lt__": lambda a, b: a.v < b.v, "__eq__": lambda a, b: a.v == b.v}))
--- check test | Many interleaved lists
(lambda lists: merge_sorted(lists) == list(range(20000)))([list(range(i, 20000, 50)) for i in range(50)])
--- check source | Uses heapq
heapq\.
--- check source absent | Does not sort everything at once
\bsorted\(|\.sort\(

+++ practice | Newest version wins
--- task
Several versions of a sensor table are kept as sorted lists of `(sensor, reading)` pairs, newest first. A reading of `None` means the sensor was removed in that version.

Write `current(versions)` that returns the current readings: a sorted list of `(sensor, reading)` pairs, where each sensor's reading comes from the newest version that mentions it, and sensors whose newest mention is `None` are left out. Use a heap to merge; ties on the sensor go to the newer version.

For example, `current([[("t1", 20)], [("t1", 18), ("t2", 5)]])` is `[("t1", 20), ("t2", 5)]`.
--- starter
import heapq


def current(versions):
    table = {}
    for version in versions:
        for sensor, reading in version:
            table[sensor] = reading
    return sorted(table.items())
--- solution
import heapq


def current(versions):
    heap = []
    iters = [iter(v) for v in versions]

    def push(i):
        pair = next(iters[i], None)
        if pair is not None:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (pair[0], i, pair[1]))

    for i in range(len(iters)):
        push(i)
    out = []
    while heap:
        sensor, i, reading = heapq.heappop(heap)
        push(i)
        while heap and heap[0][0] == sensor:
            _, j, _ = heapq.heappop(heap)
            push(j)
        if reading is not None:
            out.append((sensor, reading))
    return out
--- hint
Push `(sensor, version number, reading)` so that, for the same sensor, the newest version (the smallest number) pops first.
--- hint
After popping a sensor, pop and discard every other entry with the same sensor, refilling from their versions each time. Leave out `None` readings at the end.
--- check case | The example from the task
current([[("t1", 20)], [("t1", 18), ("t2", 5)]])
=> [("t1", 20), ("t2", 5)]
--- check case | A removal in a newer version hides an older reading
current([[("t2", None)], [("t1", 1), ("t2", 2), ("t3", 3)]])
=> [("t1", 1), ("t3", 3)]
--- check case | A reading in a newer version brings a removed sensor back
current([[("a", 9)], [("a", None)], [("a", 1)]])
=> [("a", 9)]
--- check case | No versions, and empty versions
(current([]), current([[], []]))
=> ([], [])

+++ practice | A manifest in text
--- task
A tiny store lists its live files in a text manifest: the first line is `seq=<number>`, then one file name per line, newest first, then a last line `crc=<number>` where the number is `zlib.crc32` of all the text before that line, encoded as UTF-8.

Write `write_manifest(seq, names)`, which returns the manifest text (every line ends with `"\n"`), and `read_manifest(text)`, which returns `(seq, names)`, or raises `ValueError` if the text is damaged: the last line is not a `crc=` line, the CRC does not match, or the first line is not a `seq=` line.

For example, `write_manifest(3, ["b.sst", "a.sst"])` starts with `"seq=3\nb.sst\na.sst\ncrc="`.
--- starter
import zlib


def write_manifest(seq, names):
    return f"seq={seq}\n" + "".join(n + "\n" for n in names)


def read_manifest(text):
    lines = text.split("\n")
    return int(lines[0][4:]), lines[1:-1]
--- solution
import zlib


def write_manifest(seq, names):
    body = f"seq={seq}\n" + "".join(name + "\n" for name in names)
    return body + f"crc={zlib.crc32(body.encode('utf-8'))}\n"


def read_manifest(text):
    lines = text.split("\n")
    if len(lines) < 3 or lines[-1] != "" or not lines[-2].startswith("crc="):
        raise ValueError("no checksum line")
    body = "".join(line + "\n" for line in lines[:-2])
    if lines[-2] != f"crc={zlib.crc32(body.encode('utf-8'))}":
        raise ValueError("checksum mismatch")
    if not lines[0].startswith("seq="):
        raise ValueError("no seq line")
    return int(lines[0][4:]), lines[1:-2]
--- hint
Build the body first, then compute its CRC on `body.encode("utf-8")` and add the `crc=` line.
--- hint
When reading, split on `"\n"`: a good manifest ends with an empty piece after the last newline, and the piece before it is the `crc=` line. Rebuild the body from the lines before it, and compare `crc=` lines as text.
--- check case | Round trip
read_manifest(write_manifest(3, ["b.sst", "a.sst"]))
=> (3, ["b.sst", "a.sst"])
--- check test | The exact text
write_manifest(3, ["b.sst"]) == "seq=3\nb.sst\ncrc=" + str(zlib.crc32(b"seq=3\nb.sst\n")) + "\n"
--- check case | No files
read_manifest(write_manifest(0, []))
=> (0, [])
--- check test | Damage raises ValueError
(lambda t: raises(ValueError, lambda: read_manifest(t.replace("b.sst", "c.sst"))) and raises(ValueError, lambda: read_manifest(t[:-1])) and raises(ValueError, lambda: read_manifest(t[:len(t) // 2])) and raises(ValueError, lambda: read_manifest("")))(write_manifest(3, ["b.sst", "a.sst"]))

After a crash, a folder may hold files that no longer belong to a store. Write `orphans(names, store, live)`: `names` is the list of every file in the folder, `store` is a store's name, and `live` is the list of table names its manifest holds. Return, sorted, the files to delete:

--- starter

--- solution
def orphans(names, store, live):
    live = set(live)
    doomed = []
    for name in names:
        is_table = name.startswith(store + "-") and (name.endswith(".sst") or name.endswith(".sst.tmp"))
        if (is_table and name not in live) or name == store + ".manifest.tmp":
            doomed.append(name)
    return sorted(doomed)
--- hint
`name.startswith(store)` also matches `store2-000001.sst`. Match `store + "-"` instead.
--- hint
A table is doomed only if it is not live; the manifest's temporary file is always doomed. Everything else, including the log and the manifest itself, stays.

+++ practice | Debug: the delete that did not stick
--- task
`LayeredMap` is a tiny LSM: a dict `mem` of recent writes on top of a list `tables` of older dicts, newest first. `get` checks `mem`, then the tables in order. `flush()` pushes `mem` onto the front of `tables` and starts an empty one.

The tests show a bug: deleting a key that has already been flushed does not work. The key disappears only until the next `get` looks into the tables, where the old value is still found. Fix `delete` and `get` (and anything else you need) so that a delete hides every older value, before and after a flush. `delete` returns whether the key was visible.
--- starter
class LayeredMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.mem = {}
        self.tables = []

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.mem[key] = value

    def delete(self, key):
        existed = self.get(key) is not None
        self.mem.pop(key, None)
        return existed

    def get(self, key):
        if key in self.mem:
            return self.mem[key]
        for table in self.tables:
            if key in table:
                return table[key]
        return None

    def flush(self):
        self.tables.insert(0, self.mem)
        self.mem = {}
--- solution
class LayeredMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.mem = {}
        self.tables = []

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.mem[key] = value

    def delete(self, key):
        existed = self.get(key) is not None
        self.mem[key] = None          # a tombstone hides older tables
        return existed

    def get(self, key):
        if key in self.mem:
            return self.mem[key]
        for table in self.tables:
            if key in table:
                return table[key]
        return None

    def flush(self):
        self.tables.insert(0, self.mem)
        self.mem = {}
--- hint
Removing the key from `mem` makes `get` look further down. What must `mem` hold instead, so that `get` stops there?
--- hint
Store a tombstone: `self.mem[key] = None`. Because `get` returns the first layer's value, `None` in a newer layer now means "deleted", and it survives a flush into the tables.
--- check case | A flushed key can be deleted
(lambda m: (m.put("fuel", 350), m.flush(), m.delete("fuel"), m.get("fuel"))[2:])(LayeredMap())
=> (True, None)
--- check case | The delete survives a flush
(lambda m: (m.put("fuel", 350), m.flush(), m.delete("fuel"), m.flush(), m.get("fuel"))[-1])(LayeredMap())
=> None
--- check case | Deleting an absent key, then putting it again
(lambda m: (m.delete("x"), m.put("x", 1), m.flush(), m.delete("x"), m.put("x", 2), m.get("x"))[::5])(LayeredMap())
=> (False, 2)

+++ practice | Counting across layers
--- task
A store has a memtable and tables, each a sorted list of `(key, value)` pairs where a value of `None` is a tombstone, given newest first in one list `layers`. Write `live_count(layers, lo, hi)`: how many keys `k` with `lo <= k < hi` are live, meaning that the newest layer that has `k` gives it a value that is not `None`. `lo` or `hi` may be `None` for no bound.

It must merge the layers in one pass with a heap (not build a dict of everything), and it must not look at pairs outside the range more than it needs to: start each layer at its first key `>= lo` using `bisect`.
--- starter
def live_count(layers, lo, hi):
    seen = {}
    for layer in reversed(layers):
        for key, value in layer:
            seen[key] = value
    return sum(1 for v in seen.values() if v is not None)
--- solution
import heapq
from bisect import bisect_left


def live_count(layers, lo, hi):
    heap = []
    positions = []
    for i, layer in enumerate(layers):
        start = 0 if lo is None else bisect_left(layer, (lo,))
        positions.append(start)
        if start < len(layer) and (hi is None or layer[start][0] < hi):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (layer[start][0], i))

    def advance(i):
        positions[i] += 1
        p = positions[i]
        if p < len(layers[i]) and (hi is None or layers[i][p][0] < hi):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (layers[i][p][0], i))

    count = 0
    while heap:
        key, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        value = layers[i][positions[i]][1]
        advance(i)
        while heap and heap[0][0] == key:
            _, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
            advance(j)
        if value is not None:
            count += 1
    return count
--- hint
`bisect_left(layer, (lo,))` finds the first pair whose key is at least `lo`, because a one-item tuple sorts before every longer tuple that starts with the same key.
--- hint
Keep a position per layer and push `(key, layer number)`; the smaller layer number is newer and pops first on a tie. Pop duplicates of the same key and advance their layers. Only push a pair while its key is below `hi`.
--- check case | Newest wins, and tombstones do not count
live_count([[("b", None), ("d", "4")], [("a", "1"), ("b", "2"), ("c", "3")]], None, None)
=> 3
--- check case | Only the range counts
live_count([[("b", None), ("d", "4")], [("a", "1"), ("b", "2"), ("c", "3"), ("e", "5")]], "b", "e")
=> 2
--- check case | Empty layers and an empty range
(live_count([[], []], None, None), live_count([[("a", "1")]], "a", "a"))
=> (0, 0)
--- check test | Big layers, a narrow range
(lambda layers: live_count(layers, "k05000", "k05100") == 75)([[(f"k{i:05d}", None if i % 4 == 2 else "new") for i in range(0, 10000, 2)], [(f"k{i:05d}", "old") for i in range(10000)]])

=== cap-kv-08 | Compaction and Bloom filters
--- teach
Your store is now an LSM tree: writes are cheap, and a flush writes only the memtable. But every flush adds a table, and two costs grow with them. A `get` for a key that is not in the store must look in **every** table before it can say so. And a key overwritten in ten flushes has ten copies on disk, nine of them dead. This milestone pays both debts: **compaction** merges tables, and **Bloom filters** let a lookup skip a table without reading it.

### Compaction

**Compaction** merges several tables into one. It is milestone 7's `merge_runs` again: merge the tables newest first, keep only the newest version of each key, write the result as one new table, point the manifest at it, and delete the old tables. Afterwards a lookup has fewer tables to search, and the dead copies are gone.

The steps, and their crash points, follow the same pattern as a flush:

1. Write the merged table, numbered `next_table`, with `write_sstable`. A crash here leaves an orphan, which recovery deletes; the old tables are still named by the manifest.
2. Write the manifest with the new table in place of the merged ones. This rename is the commit point.
3. Delete the merged tables. A crash here leaves them as orphans, which recovery deletes.

The merged table gets the `seq` of the newest table in the merge, so the manifest's seq never goes backwards.

### When a tombstone may go

Compaction is the only place tombstones can finally be thrown away, and it is where the most dangerous LSM bug lives.

A tombstone exists to hide older versions of its key. Suppose there are three tables, newest first: `t3` holds a tombstone for `fuel`, `t2` does not mention `fuel`, and `t1` holds `fuel = 350`. Compact only `t3` and `t2`, and drop the tombstone because "the key is deleted anyway": the merged table no longer mentions `fuel`, the next lookup falls through to `t1`, and `fuel = 350` is **back from the dead**.

The rule: **a compaction may drop tombstones only when it includes the oldest table**, because only then is there nothing below it left to hide. `compact(count)` merges the newest `count` tables; when that is all of them, tombstones go. This gives an invariant worth knowing by name: **the oldest table holds no tombstones**. A flush onto a store with no tables already respected it; now a compaction of every table does too.

### Choosing what to compact

The simplest policy compacts every table each time there are more than `max_tables` of them. That keeps reads fast, but each compaction rewrites the whole store: after a million keys, every flush of a hundred new keys would rewrite a million. The total work of writing grows like O(n²).

**Size-tiered compaction** merges tables of similar size. Starting from the newest table, keep adding the next older one while it is at most twice the size of everything taken so far; stop at the first table that is much bigger. Small recent tables are merged often and cheaply, and a big old table is rewritten only when enough data has piled up on top of it to be worth it. Then each entry is rewritten about O(log n) times over its life, not O(n) times. The [[amplification|amplification]] note puts numbers on it.

```text
tables (entries), newest first:   3   2   4   40
take 3; next is 2 <= 2*3: take;   next is 4 <= 2*5: take;   next is 40 > 2*9: stop
-> compact the newest 3 tables into one of 9; the 40-entry table is untouched
```

LevelDB and RocksDB use a different policy, **leveled** compaction, which keeps the tables of each level free of overlapping key ranges. It reads less and writes more. Both are real choices that real engines let their users make.

### Bloom filters

Compaction cuts the number of tables, but a store always has a few, and a `get` for a missing key still reads a block of each. A **Bloom filter** answers "is this key definitely not in this table?" from a small bit array kept in memory, without reading the table at all.

A Bloom filter is an array of m bits, all 0 at first, and k hash functions. To **add** a key, compute its k hash positions and set those bits to 1. To **test** a key, compute the same positions: if any of those bits is 0, the key was never added, **definitely**. If all are 1, the key was **probably** added: the bits might have been set by other keys. So a Bloom filter has no false negatives and a small rate of false positives. The [[false positive rate|fp-rate]] note has the formula; with 10 bits per key and k = 7, about 1 lookup in 120 of a missing key gets a wrong "probably".

```python fragment
position = (h1 + i * h2) % bits       # the i-th of the k positions
array[position >> 3] |= 1 << (position & 7)
```

Where do k hash functions come from? **Double hashing**: compute two big hashes h1 and h2 of the key once, and use h1 + i·h2 for i = 0 … k − 1. That is known to work as well as k independent hashes for a Bloom filter. This store takes both from `hashlib.blake2b` with a 16-byte digest: the first 8 bytes are h1, the last 8 are h2 (made odd, so it can never be 0). Position p is bit `p & 7` of byte `p >> 3`.

Why not Python's own `hash()`? Because for strings it is **randomised per process**: run the program twice and `hash("fuel")` differs. A filter written to a table by one run would give false **negatives** in the next, silently hiding data. A filter stored in a file needs a hash that is the same forever.

### A second table format

Each table now carries its filter. `write_sstable` adds every key (tombstones too, since a tombstone is an answer) to a filter sized with `BloomFilter.for_keys(n)`, and writes the filter's bytes between the index and the footer. The footer grows to record where the filter is, its size and its CRC, and the magic becomes `b"KVSST002"`, so that a reader can never mistake one format for the other. Opening a table loads the filter and checks it; `get` asks the filter first and counts the lookups it saved in `bloom_skips`.

A filter only helps point lookups. A scan wants every key in a range, and a filter cannot list keys.

### Seeing inside

Two more methods make the structure visible. `explain(key)` says, layer by layer, how a `get` would be answered: "memtable: not there", "db-000004.sst: Bloom filter says no", "db-000001.sst: found". It is the kind of tool that turns a baffling bug into an obvious one. And `backup(dest)` copies the store to another file system: a checkpoint first, then the tables and the manifest. Because tables never change once written, the copy is consistent without stopping anything, which is how real LSM stores take backups.

### Why it is correct

Compaction keeps "newest wins" true: `merge_runs` keeps each key's newest version among the merged tables, and the merged table takes their place in the same position in the stack, so every lookup finds the same answer as before. Dropping tombstones changes nothing visible only when no older table remains below, which is exactly the rule. The Bloom filter never changes an answer, because it never says "no" to a key that was added.

### What it costs

- A compaction of tables holding N entries in all: O(N log t) to merge t tables, and O(N) written.
- With size-tiered compaction, each entry is written O(log n) times in total, instead of O(n).
- A Bloom filter: m bits, about 10 per key, 1.25 bytes; a test costs k hash positions from one hash computation.
- A `get` for a missing key: nearly always zero table reads, instead of one block per table.

### Where it is used

Every LSM engine compacts: Cassandra offers size-tiered and leveled strategies, RocksDB leveled and universal (a size-tiered variant). Bigtable, HBase, LevelDB and RocksDB keep a Bloom filter per table. Burton Bloom invented the filter in 1970 to spell-check with less memory; today [[Bloom filters|bloom-uses]] also appear in browsers, networks and caches.

**Watch out:** dropping tombstones in a compaction that leaves an older table untouched, which brings deleted data back; building a filter with `hash()`, which forgets everything at the next restart; deleting the old tables before the manifest names the new one; and trusting a filter's "probably" as "yes": after a filter says maybe, the table must still be read.

::: context amplification Counting the rewrites
Write amplification is the number of bytes written to disk for each byte the user writes. With full compaction on every flush, a store of n entries rewrites all n each time, so after n flushes of one entry each, it has written about n²/2 entries. With size-tiered compaction and a size ratio of 2, an entry is merged into a table roughly twice its size each time it is rewritten, so it can be rewritten only about log2 n times before its table holds everything. For a million entries that is about 20 rewrites per entry instead of about half a million.
:::

::: context fp-rate How often a filter is wrong
After n keys are added to m bits with k hashes, the chance that a given bit is still 0 is about e to the power −kn/m. A missing key is a false positive when all k of its bits are 1, which happens with probability about (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. For a fixed m/n, the best k is (m/n)·ln 2. With 10 bits per key that is k ≈ 7 and a rate of about 0.8%; each extra bit per key roughly cuts the rate by a third. A filter with 16 bits per key is wrong about once in 2,000 lookups.
:::

::: context bloom-uses A small set that may say yes wrongly
Burton Bloom's 1970 paper proposed the filter for hyphenating words with little memory: keep the rare words in a filter, and look up the dictionary on disk only when the filter says maybe. The same pattern, a cheap in-memory test in front of an expensive lookup, is everywhere: web caches use filters to skip caching pages seen only once, Bitcoin clients used them to ask for relevant transactions, and databases use them to avoid reading from disk. When a false positive costs a little extra work and a false negative would cost correctness, a Bloom filter fits.
:::
--- task
The starter keeps milestones 1 to 7 and adds stubs. Add `import hashlib` at the top of the file. Then write:

`BloomFilter(bits, hashes, data=None)`: raise `ValueError` if `bits` or `hashes` is below 1. Attributes `bits`, `hashes` and `array`, a `bytearray` of `(bits + 7) // 8` zero bytes, or a copy of `data` when it is given. `BloomFilter.for_keys(n, bits_per_key=10)` (a class method) returns a filter with `max(64, n * bits_per_key)` bits and `max(1, round(bits_per_key * 0.69))` hashes. The positions of a key: `digest = hashlib.blake2b(key.encode("utf-8"), digest_size=16).digest()`, `h1 = int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "little")`, `h2 = int.from_bytes(digest[8:], "little") | 1`, and position i is `(h1 + i * h2) % bits` for i from 0 to `hashes - 1`. Bit p is bit `p & 7` of byte `p >> 3`. `add(key)` sets the key's bits; `key in bf` is `True` when all of them are set.

The table format, version 2: `SST_MAGIC = b"KVSST002"` and `SST_FOOTER = struct.Struct("<8sQQQQIQIIII")`, packing magic, index offset, index entries, entry count, seq, index CRC, bloom offset, bloom bits, bloom hashes, bloom CRC and footer CRC. `write_sstable` builds `BloomFilter.for_keys(number of entries)`, adds every key (tombstones too) and writes the filter's `array` right after the index. `SSTable` checks that the filter's CRC matches and that its length is `(bits + 7) // 8` (else `CorruptFile`), keeps it as `bloom`, and has a counter `bloom_skips`; `get` returns `None` at once, adding 1 to `bloom_skips`, when the key is not in the filter.

In `KVStore`:

- The constructor becomes `KVStore(fs, name="db", wal_limit=None, max_tables=None, index_every=16, seed=0)`, with attributes `max_tables` and `compactions` (compactions run since opening, starting at 0).
- `compact(count=None)`: merge the newest `count` tables (all of them when `None`), as in the lesson. Do nothing unless `2 <= count <= len(tables)`. Otherwise add 1 to `compactions`; drop tombstones only if every table is in the merge; write the merged entries (if there are any) as table number `next_table` with the newest merged table's `seq`; put it where the merged tables were; write the manifest; then delete the merged tables' files.
- After every flush: if `max_tables` is not `None` and there are more tables than that, compact by the size-tiered rule of the lesson, counting sizes in entries (`len(table)`), and merging at least 2 tables.
- `explain(key)`: a list of lines. If the memtable has the key: just `["memtable: found"]` or `["memtable: tombstone"]`. Otherwise `"memtable: not there"`, then for each table, newest first, `f"{name}: Bloom filter says no"`, `f"{name}: not there (Bloom filter false positive)"`, or `f"{name}: found"` / `f"{name}: tombstone"` (stop there); if no table has it, a last line `"not found"`.
- `backup(dest)`: checkpoint, then copy every table's bytes and then the manifest's to the file system `dest` with `write_atomically`, under the same names.
--- starter
"""A key-value store with a write-ahead log, crash recovery and a query language.

The layers, from the bottom up:

  records      the binary record: length, CRC32 checksum, sequence number
  MemFS        a simulated file system that can crash after any byte
  KVStore      an in-memory table, made durable by a write-ahead log
  SSTable      a sorted, immutable file with an index
  SkipList     the sorted in-memory table, for range scans
  LSM tree     the memtable flushes to SSTables listed in a manifest
"""
from bisect import bisect_right
import heapq
import random
import struct
import zlib
from typing import NamedTuple


# ===========================================================================
# Records
# ===========================================================================
# Every file this store writes is made of records. On disk, one record is:
#
#     length   u32   how many bytes the body has
#     crc      u32   zlib.crc32 of the body
#     body:
#       seq    u64   sequence number: 1, 2, 3, ... in the order written
#       kind   u8    what the record does: PUT, DELETE, ...
#       klen   u32   length of the key in bytes (UTF-8)
#       vlen   u32   length of the value in bytes (UTF-8)
#       key    klen bytes
#       value  vlen bytes
#
# All integers are little-endian ("<" in struct).

HEADER = struct.Struct("<II")    # length, crc
BODY = struct.Struct("<QBII")    # seq, kind, klen, vlen
MAX_BODY = 1 << 24               # 16 MiB: a longer body is damage, not data

PUT = 1
DELETE = 2
KINDS = {PUT, DELETE}


class Record(NamedTuple):
    seq: int
    kind: int
    key: str
    value: str = ""


class RecordError(Exception):
    """The bytes at an offset are not one whole, valid record."""


class TornRecord(RecordError):
    """The data ends before the record does: the last write was cut short."""


class CorruptRecord(RecordError):
    """All of the record's bytes are there, but they are damaged."""


def encode_record(record):
    """The bytes of one record: the header, then the body."""
    key = record.key.encode("utf-8")
    value = record.value.encode("utf-8")
    body = BODY.pack(record.seq, record.kind, len(key), len(value)) + key + value
    if len(body) > MAX_BODY:
        # Never write what decode_record would reject: it would be lost.
        raise ValueError(f"record of {len(body)} bytes is larger than {MAX_BODY}")
    return HEADER.pack(len(body), zlib.crc32(body)) + body


def decode_record(data, offset=0):
    """Decode the record that starts at data[offset].

    Returns (record, end), where end is the offset just past the record.
    Raises TornRecord if the data stops before the record ends, and
    CorruptRecord if the record is complete but fails a check.
    """
    left = len(data) - offset
    if left < HEADER.size:
        raise TornRecord(f"offset {offset}: {left} of {HEADER.size} header bytes")
    length, crc = HEADER.unpack_from(data, offset)
    if length < BODY.size or length > MAX_BODY:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: impossible body length {length}")
    start = offset + HEADER.size
    end = start + length
    if end > len(data):
        raise TornRecord(f"offset {offset}: body of {length} bytes, {len(data) - start} there")
    body = bytes(data[start:end])
    if zlib.crc32(body) != crc:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: checksum mismatch")
    seq, kind, klen, vlen = BODY.unpack_from(body)
    if kind not in KINDS:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: unknown kind {kind}")
    if BODY.size + klen + vlen != length:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: key and value lengths do not add up")
    try:
        key = body[BODY.size:BODY.size + klen].decode("utf-8")
        value = body[BODY.size + klen:].decode("utf-8")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        raise CorruptRecord(f"offset {offset}: text is not valid UTF-8") from None
    return Record(seq, kind, key, value), end


def read_records(data):
    """Decode records from the start of data, stopping at the first bad one.

    Returns (records, good_end, problem). good_end is the offset just past
    the last good record. problem is None when all of data was good, "torn"
    when it ends in a cut-off record, and "corrupt" when a record is damaged.
    """
    records = []
    offset = 0
    while offset < len(data):
        try:
            record, end = decode_record(data, offset)
        except TornRecord:
            return records, offset, "torn"
        except CorruptRecord:
            return records, offset, "corrupt"
        records.append(record)
        offset = end
    return records, offset, None


# ===========================================================================
# A file system that can crash
# ===========================================================================
class SimulatedCrash(Exception):
    """The simulated machine died in the middle of an operation.

    Store code must never catch this: a real crash cannot be caught either.
    """


class MemFS:
    """An in-memory file system that can crash after any byte.

    Every byte written is one step, and so is each sync, rename, truncate
    and delete. With budget=k exactly k steps happen: the machine crashes
    when step k + 1 is tried, part-way through a write if need be.
    budget=None never crashes. `steps` counts the steps taken, so one run
    with no budget measures a workload.

    The program sees every byte it has written. crash() gives the files a
    restarted machine finds: every written byte after a process crash, only
    the synced bytes after a power loss.
    """

    def __init__(self, budget=None):
        self.files = {}      # name -> bytearray: what the program sees
        self.synced = {}     # name -> how many leading bytes are durable
        self.budget = budget
        self.steps = 0
        self.crashed = False

    # -- the crash machinery ------------------------------------------------

    def _allow(self, n):
        """Take up to n steps; return how many the budget allows."""
        if self.crashed:
            raise SimulatedCrash("the machine has already crashed")
        if self.budget is None:
            allowed = n
        else:
            allowed = max(0, min(n, self.budget - self.steps))
        self.steps += allowed
        return allowed

    def _die(self):
        self.crashed = True
        raise SimulatedCrash(f"crashed after {self.steps} steps")

    def _step(self):
        if self._allow(1) < 1:
            self._die()

    def _need(self, name):
        if name not in self.files:
            raise FileNotFoundError(name)

    # -- reading costs no steps --------------------------------------------

    def exists(self, name):
        return name in self.files

    def names(self):
        return sorted(self.files)

    def size(self, name):
        self._need(name)
        return len(self.files[name])

    def read(self, name):
        self._need(name)
        return bytes(self.files[name])

    def read_at(self, name, offset, size):
        """Up to size bytes from offset on (fewer at the end of the file)."""
        self._need(name)
        return bytes(self.files[name][offset:offset + size])

    # -- writing: every byte and every operation is a step -----------------

    def append(self, name, data):
        """Add bytes to the end of a file, creating it if needed."""
        allowed = self._allow(len(data))
        if name not in self.files:
            self.files[name] = bytearray()
            self.synced[name] = 0
        self.files[name] += data[:allowed]
        if allowed < len(data):
            self._die()

    def sync(self, name):
        """Make every byte written to the file so far durable (fsync)."""
        self._need(name)
        self._step()
        self.synced[name] = len(self.files[name])

    def rename(self, old, new):
        """Give a file a new name in one atomic step, replacing any file there."""
        self._need(old)
        self._step()
        self.files[new] = self.files.pop(old)
        self.synced[new] = self.synced.pop(old)

    def truncate(self, name, size):
        """Cut a file down to its first size bytes."""
        self._need(name)
        if not 0 <= size <= len(self.files[name]):
            raise ValueError(f"cannot truncate {name} to {size} bytes")
        self._step()
        del self.files[name][size:]
        self.synced[name] = min(self.synced[name], size)

    def delete(self, name):
